title: EN 18286:2026, AI Quality Management for the EU AI Act
subtitle: The first harmonised standard under the EU AI Act, for the Article 17 quality management system

The one-paragraph answer

EN 18286:2026, Artificial intelligence, Quality management system for EU AI Act regulatory purposes, is the European standard from CEN and CENELEC for the quality management system that Article 17 of the EU AI Act requires of every provider of a high-risk AI system. It is the first harmonised standard under the Act: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274 published its reference in the Official Journal of the European Union on 14 October 2026, and the decision took effect that day. A provider that follows a harmonised standard is presumed to conform with the requirements the standard covers. It is written to sit on top of an existing management system such as ISO/IEC 42001 or ISO 9001, not to replace it.

What EN 18286 is

EN 18286 is a European Norm, adopted jointly by the European Committee for Standardization (CEN) and the European Committee for Electrotechnical Standardization (CENELEC). The Commission asked the two bodies for it in its 2025 standardisation request for the AI Act, Implementing Decision C(2025) 3871 of 23 June 2025, as the deliverable on quality management systems for providers of AI systems, including post-market monitoring processes (point 9 of Annex I to that request, as the citing decision records).

Its intended users are providers of high-risk AI systems, the organisations that develop a high-risk system or have one developed and place it on the market under their own name. A deployer that only uses a high-risk system is not the audience, though it will meet the standard in its suppliers' documentation.

Because a harmonised standard is how European product law turns legal requirements into something an auditor can test, CEN and CENELEC called EN 18286 a landmark when it was cited, and described it as translating the Article 17 requirements into practical, auditable requirements that providers can apply.

The Official Journal citation

A European Norm becomes a harmonised standard with legal effect only when the Commission publishes its reference in the Official Journal. For EN 18286 that step is Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274 of 12 October 2026 on the harmonised standards for high-risk AI systems drafted in support of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, published in the L series of the Official Journal as 2026/2274 on 14 October 2026. Its annex lists one standard, EN 18286:2026. Article 2 of the decision puts it into force on the day of publication, and the decision's recitals record that the Commission assessed the standard with CEN and CENELEC and found that it satisfies the requirements it aims to cover.

Pages written before 14 October 2026, including earlier text on this site, describe the citation as pending. It is no longer pending. CEN and CENELEC announced it on 15 October, noting that it coincided with World Standards Day, and the Commission's own announcement on its digital strategy site is dated later still, which is why some reports give a later date. The date that counts is the Official Journal's, 14 October 2026.

What it covers: the Article 17 quality management system

Article 17(1) of the AI Act requires providers of high-risk AI systems to put in place a quality management system that ensures compliance with the Regulation, documented as written policies, procedures and instructions. It lists thirteen aspects the system must include at least: a strategy for regulatory compliance, including conformity assessment and the management of modifications; design, design control and design verification; development, quality control and quality assurance; examination, test and validation before, during and after development; the technical specifications and standards applied; data management across acquisition, labelling, storage, retention and the rest; the risk management system of Article 9; post-market monitoring under Article 72; serious incident reporting under Article 73; communication with authorities, notified bodies, other operators and customers; record-keeping; resource management, including security of supply; and an accountability framework for management and staff.

EN 18286 is the standard written to meet that list. Article 17(2), as amended in 2026, adds that the system should be proportionate to the size of the provider, with SMEs, start-ups and small mid-caps named, without lowering the rigour needed for compliance.

The quality management system obligation in Article 17 sits in Chapter III, Section 3 of the Act. In the consolidated text of 27 July 2026, that section applies from 2 December 2027 for high-risk systems under Annex III and from 2 August 2028 for those under Annex I. A provider therefore has the standard more than a year before the obligation applies, which is roughly the time a management system needs to run before it has records worth auditing.

What the presumption does and does not cover

Article 40(1) of the Act presumes conformity for systems that follow a harmonised standard cited in the Official Journal, "to the extent that those standards cover" the requirements. The presumption is therefore only as wide as the standard's own declared coverage, which a harmonised standard sets out in its Annex Z table.

Two points are worth checking with counsel rather than assuming. First, in the consolidated text of 27 July 2026, Article 40(1) ties the presumption to the requirements in Chapter III, Section 2 (Articles 8 to 15) and to the general-purpose model obligations in Chapter V, while Article 17 sits in Section 3; CEN and CENELEC describe the citation as giving presumption of conformity with the corresponding provisions of the Act. Second, Modulos, a governance software company that has published a reading of the standard, says its Annex ZA maps clauses to Article 17(1) and to the first sentence of Article 11(1) on technical documentation, and marks Article 17(2) to 17(4) as not covered. Those are Modulos's reading of a document we have not read, not ours and not the Commission's.

A presumption of conformity is also not a certificate. It is a legal presumption that a market surveillance authority can rebut, and the provider still carries out the conformity assessment the Act requires for its system.

How EN 18286 relates to ISO/IEC 42001 and ISO 9001

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is the international, certifiable standard for an AI management system, structured around the organisation and every AI system it develops, provides or uses. EN 18286 is structured around the high-risk AI system and the regulation's requirements for it. The two do different jobs: 42001 earns a certificate from an accredited certification body; EN 18286, once cited, earns a legal presumption under EU law for what it covers.

According to Modulos's reading, EN 18286 carries an annex giving the correspondence of its clauses with ISO 9001:2015 and another with ISO/IEC 42001, and it states that the correspondence is of clauses only, not of requirements, and does not make the standards equivalent. The practical consequence is the one most providers will care about: an organisation that already runs ISO/IEC 42001 or ISO 9001 extends that system to meet EN 18286 rather than building a second one, but holding a 42001 certificate does not by itself show conformity with EN 18286 or with Article 17.

Providers already bound by a quality management system under sectoral EU law, such as medical device makers, may include the Article 17 aspects in that system; Article 17(3) of the Act allows it. Under Article 17(4), a financial institution meets most of the obligation through its internal governance rules under EU financial services law, except for risk management, post-market monitoring and incident reporting, and harmonised standards are to be taken into account. The NIST AI RMF remains a voluntary US framework with no presumption of anything under EU law, though its Govern and Manage functions cover much of the same ground. These comparisons are ours.

How to put EN 18286 to work: a 5-step path

These steps are our own practical sequence for a provider that has just heard the standard was cited. They are not drawn from the standard's text.

  1. Confirm you are a provider of a high-risk system. Classify each AI system against Article 6 and Annexes I and III. The Article 17 obligation, and so the standard, applies to providers of high-risk systems; a deployer meets it through its suppliers.
  2. Get a licensed copy. EN 18286 is sold through national standards bodies in each country's adopted edition. This page does not summarise its clauses and cannot stand in for it.
  3. Gap-assess the system you already run. Map an existing ISO/IEC 42001, ISO 9001 or sector quality system against the standard and against the thirteen aspects of Article 17(1), and record each gap with an owner.
  4. Read the Annex ZA table before you rely on the presumption. Note which provisions the standard declares it covers, and how you will show conformity for anything it does not.
  5. Start producing records now. Article 17 applies from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems. A quality system is credible to an assessor when it has months of design reviews, test results, incident logs and post-market monitoring behind it, not when it was written the week before.

Frequently asked questions about EN 18286

Is EN 18286 a harmonised standard under the EU AI Act?

Yes. Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274 published its reference in the Official Journal on 14 October 2026, which makes it the first harmonised standard supporting the AI Act.

Does following EN 18286 make a provider compliant with Article 17?

It gives a presumption of conformity with the requirements the standard covers, which a regulator can rebut. Check the standard's Annex ZA for the coverage it declares; a reading published by Modulos says Article 17(2) to 17(4) are marked as not covered.

Can a company be certified to EN 18286?

The presumption comes from applying the standard, not from a certificate. Certification bodies may offer audits against it, but under the AI Act what matters is the provider's conformity assessment of its high-risk system. Certification to ISO/IEC 42001 is a separate thing.

Does an ISO/IEC 42001 certificate count?

Not on its own. ISO/IEC 42001 is international, organisation-wide and not a harmonised standard. EN 18286 is built to be layered on top of it, so an existing 42001 system is a strong starting point.

When does the obligation apply?

The Article 17 quality management system obligation applies from 2 December 2027 for high-risk systems under Annex III and from 2 August 2028 for those under Annex I, in the consolidated text of 27 July 2026.

Are more harmonised standards coming?

Yes. CEN and CENELEC's joint technical committee is drafting further standards in response to the same request, on subjects CEN and CENELEC list as including risk management, conformity assessment, datasets, bias, cybersecurity, robustness and logging. Each becomes harmonised only when its own reference is published in the Official Journal. This site's standards watch records any act that amends or corrects Decision 2026/2274.

How this page was written

This page was drafted with AI assistance from sources the editor read on 24 October 2026: the text of Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274 and the consolidated AI Act of 27 July 2026, both retrieved from the EU Publications Office; CEN and CENELEC's announcement of 15 October 2026; and Modulos's published reading of the standard. CEN and CENELEC's standards catalogue disallows automated reading in its robots.txt and was not read; the approval date comes from this site's earlier record of the catalogue entry and from Modulos. We have not read the standard itself. Nothing on this page quotes, summarises or paraphrases its clauses, and statements about its annexes are attributed to Modulos.
